In fact, the analysis of the effects in crystalline Li2O confirmed that H is neither bonding to surface atoms nor creating a compound. Rather, the incident H is retained in the potential minima of the typical multi-atom – multi-coordinated configurations. The results that were obtained in an amorphous Li-O slab are, in part, smeared “versions” of the effects of the atom configurations shown for the Li2O crystal. The DFT geometry optimizations of a number of “seeded” H atoms in a small, 2x2x2 superlattice of Li2O showed that H atoms close to the symmetry center of the lattice occupies a multi-coordinated potential minimum, similarly as found with the ReaxFF calculations in a Li2O crystal. However, some H atoms acquired a positive charge in the process of the DFT geometry optimization. Interestingly, the SCC-DFTB calculations give a different picture of the bonding chemistry of H in an  a:Li2O surface, in which  many H atoms get a positive charge and are bonded to the resident oxygen atoms, and only a few H atoms are bonded  to Li atoms, and some  possibly create V-shaped LiOH molecules. The DFT calculations with a Li2O crystal agree well with the ReaxFF results, while the DFTB calculations indicate that all H atoms get charged positive and strongly bond to oxygens. Thus, the potential field of ReaxFF leads to an acceptable description of the H chemistry, while DFTB leads, in this case, to a qualitatively wrong picture of the bonding interplay between H, Li and O. Obviously, the over-bonding potential field resulting from the existing Li-O-H pair potentials in DFTB is not accurate enough to create correct interparticle dynamics. Varying concentration ratios of O, Li, and H and observing resultant atomic charging indicate that the surface chemistry might also strongly depend on the proportion of the Li-O-H constituents. The importance of inclusion of atomic charging for the system chemistry is further stressed by the results of CMD/ReaxFF calculations with the exclusion of charges in LAMMPS. This leads to  completely different particle dynamics and an inadequate bonding chemistry. In spite of the current success of the ReaxFF potential, we see space for further improvement, as indicated by the DFT Li2O cluster calculations. This can be done by replacing the EEM charging dynamics with ACKS2 [36], which has the potential to better describe the charging boundary conditions of the impact H particle and, thus, a better description of the chemistry at the top layer of the surface. In the case of the amorphous LiOH (a:LiOH) surface, an impacting H atom acquires a balanced number of positive and negative charges, which create with the resident atoms water, OH radicals, lithium-hydride, and hydrogen molecules, and likely takes a part in recreating LiOH molecules. This picture is qualitatively similar to the one obtained by the QCMD/DFTB approach. Since the process of accumulation of hydrogen in the surface changes its content by both volumetric concentration and by a possible chain of chemical processes described here, it is important for a final understanding of these processes to consider the chemical evolution of the surface during H accumulation, which will be a subject of our future research.

## ABSTRACT

Detailed experimental and computational information on the response of lithium surfaces to irradiation by slow hydrogenic particles (ions, atoms, molecules) is sparse and mainly speculative. In this work, we present a computational study of the reflection and retention of deuterium (D) atoms at crystalline and amorphous lithium surfaces at 300 and 500 K, where the D atoms have an impact energy in the range of 0.025–5 eV and incident angles of 0° (perpendicular incidence) or 85° (near-grazing incidence). Classical molecular dynamics simulations are performed with the reactive bond-order force field (ReaxFF) potentials. This study provides quantitative information on the deuterium sticking probability and recycling coefficient for lithium surfaces. Our results support the ongoing work at the Lithium Tokamak eXperiment-β fusion experiment as well as relevant experiments in the laboratory setting.

I. INTRODUCTION

The use of lithium as a plasma-facing material has been investigated in various devices such as the Lithium Tokamak eXperiment (LTX),1 National Spherical Torus eXperiment (NSTX),2 EAST,3

HIDRA,4 and STOR-M.5 Researchers at LTX at the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory reported improved plasma performance and a flat electron temperature profile due to a lowering of the hydrogen recycling coefficient (Rw), which is the ratio of the flux of ejected hydrogen atoms from the wall to the flux of incident hydrogen ions and atoms from the plasma.1,6 Hydrogen recycling at Li plasma-facing components is a complex function of many variables including the Li oxidation state, uptake of H in the Li surface, surface temperature of the wall, and incident energy of hydrogen.7–13

There is still much to be learned about the plasma–material interactions at Li surfaces in order to optimize plasma performance. The electron temperature in LTX plasmas reaches 100–300 eV in the core and into the edge, although neutral gas temperatures (Tg) near the edge are closer to the wall temperature (<1000 K).14

In the neutral gas temperature range Tg < 1 eV, which is typical in fusion devices, lithium readily absorbs atomic hydrogen much more than diatomic hydrogen because for diatomic hydrogen to be

absorbed in lithium, it must dissociate into atomic hydrogen.15 The bond dissociation energy of H2 is 4.5 eV,16 making non-catalytic dissociation unlikely for H2 impacts at Tg < 1 eV. The kinetics of hydrogen sorption by lithium typically involves the sticking coefficient, which is defined as

S(E, θ, T) ¼ NS(E, θ, T) Ni(E, θ) , (1)

where NS is the number of particles retained by the lithium surface, Ni is the number of impacting particles at the surface, E is the incident energy, θ is the incident angle, and T is the surface temperature.17–22 It is important to define the surface as the transition region between the material bulk and the vacuum, which could have a thickness from nm to μm, depending on the observed process and particle incident energy. It is important to distinguish the structure of lithium as amorphous (solid or liquid) or crystalline in order to establish possible roles that the Li surface structure can play in hydrogen recycling. Due to the large particle fluxes and wide energy and angular ranges of particles irradiating the walls in a fusion reactor, it is commonly

Thus, on a microscopic scale relevant to this work, the surface of the lithium deposited inside fusion devices is expected to be amorphous, consisting of peaks and valleys at nm to μm scales due to the roughness of an underlying solid substrate or deposition, ejection, and bubble formation mechanisms of liquid metals.23,24

Amorphous systems can possess spatial variability in bond parameters, leading to local differences in surface reactivity.25 For those reasons, we selected an amorphous Li surface as our primary target, although we also report herein studies of D atom interactions with a pristine crystalline surface. Tokamak divertors typically employ grazing incident angles of the magnetic field at the surface (≈90° from the surface normal). Hence, H atoms can also be anisotropically oriented to a grazing incidence angle due to charge exchange reactions with ions, which move toward the surface in a gyro motion along the B-field. This anisotropic velocity distribution of H atoms and the surface roughness gives rise to a variety of incident angles of H atoms impinging at the surface. The molecular dynamics (MD) method used in this work to simulate the irradiation process of atomic deuterium on amorphous and crystalline lithium surfaces is briefly described in Sec. II. Our results are presented and discussed in Sec. III. Finally, our conclusions are provided in Sec. IV.

II. COMPUTATIONAL METHOD

Modeling was done by implementing the bond order-based force field ReaxFF26 in the molecular dynamics simulator LAMMPS (LargeScale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator).27 Due to the large difference in the electronegativities of Li (0.98) and H (2.2),28,29 the bonding between Li and H is mixed ionic-covalent, which is carefully taken into account by ReaxFF. This approach to modeling Li-H systems was verified in previous research performed by Krstić et al.30–33 The simulations presented in this work utilized one of two different Li surface targets: (1) a slab with a monocrystalline BCC structure [Li(100) surface34]; lattice constant 3.609 Å or (2) a slab with an amorphous

structure. The crystalline slab, after 3D energy minimization, thermalization to the surface temperatures (TLi) of 300 and 500 K, and relaxation to the surface boundary conditions and 2D periodicity, occupied a box of approximate dimensions 7.8 × 7.8 × 2 nm3, containing 5000 7Li atoms (Fig. 1). Amorphization of the crystalline slab was done using the usual procedure, by repeatedly fast heating to 5000 K and slow annealing to 300 K with 3D periodicity, followed by relaxation to the surface boundary conditions and 2D periodicity (in the x- and y-directions). The final bounding box of the amorphous slab at 300 K had approximate dimensions of 8 × 8 × 2 nm3 and contained 5000 atoms. The mass densities of both crystalline and amorphous slabs were about 0.5 g/cm3, close to the densities of bulk solid and liquid lithium. The surface was thermalized as a NVE (microcanonical) ensemble by a Langevin thermostat with a time constant of 100 fs. In the following discussions, we will utilize the nomenclature c:Li and a:Li as shorthand for the crystalline Li surface and the amorphous Li surface, respectively. The Lindeman index17 of the considered Li slabs was calculated over 5000 one-fs steps at 300 and 400 K (crystalline surface) and 500 and 600 K (amorphous surface) (see Fig. 2). The sharp increase in the Lindemann index between 400 and 500 K indicates the typical phase transition for Li from solid to liquid between 400 and 500 K (Li melting point is 453 K at 1 atm). A commonly accepted criterion for a liquid phase is a Lindemann index of  0:1, which is approximately achieved (>0.07) in spite of our relatively small slab. We will consider the results obtained with 500 K amorphous lithium surfaces as valid for liquid Li. In Sec. III, we also provide results for amorphous and crystalline Li slabs at 300 K. We examined the H impact energy (E) range of 0.025–5 eV, which is relevant for tokamak reactors, and impact angles (θ) of 0° and 85° (measured from the surface normal) to investigate the sensitivity of H sticking on the impact angle. Given a set of input parameters, including θ and E, individual runs were performed with deuterium atoms impacting the surface, scanning the surface uniformly with N = 1023 trajectories at different impact points (x, y) for each particle. The data from each trajectory were collected and analyzed for each input set. If Ns is the number of successful trajectories (Ns ≤N) and n is a sampled size of desired outcome O, then the probability of O per impact atom is PO = nO/Ns, with a standard error SEO given by SEO ¼ PO/ ﬃﬃﬃﬃ no p .18

So, the reflection probability is PR = nR/Ns, while the probability of sticking [Eq. (1)] of D per impact is Pret = 1 −PR. The size of a time step in MD depends primarily on the impact energy. For the very small impact energies considered in this work, the time step of 1 fs for E  0:1 eV and 0.5 fs for E > 0.1 eV was satisfactory. The number of time steps per single trajectory depends on both the impact energy and the incident angle. Since all trajectories have started from about 1 nm above the surface, the number of time steps steeply increased with incident angle. For θ = 85°, the number of time steps for an impact energy of 0.05 eV was typically 8000. The needed number of steps increases steeply with a further increase in the incident angle, which becomes computationally formidable. However, for orthogonal impact (θ = 0°), the typical number of time steps was about 3000 at E = 0.05 eV. In the case of singly charged ions impinging on a metal surface, it is assumed that the ions are neutralized at asymptotic distances by electrons from the Fermi sea of the metal target before reaching the surface. Consequently, impacts of neutral D atoms effectively capture the behavior of impinging D ions, as confirmed by a number of experiments.7,9,10,17,18 Our calculations assumed a single atom hitting a surface. No effects due to the accumulation of D at the surface were taken into account, which will be a subject of our future studies.

II, the probabilities of reflection (PR) are calculated for each impact energy and incident angle as a ratio of the number of reflected trajectories (NR) and the total number of successful trajectories (NS), with PR = NR/NS. The probabilities of sticking (retention) per D impact, Pret, are in all cases defined by particle conservation, i.e., Pret= 1 −PR, and therefore do not need to be separately discussed.

IV. CONCLUSIONS

In this work, we utilized molecular dynamics simulations to study the sticking probability of incident D atoms (E = 0.025–5 eV; θ = 0° or 85° measured from the surface normal) on crystalline and amorphous Li surfaces at 300 or 500 K. Our results revealed slightly higher reflection probabilities (and lower sticking probabilities) for deuterium at lithium surfaces in an amorphous (liquid) lithium state (500 K), which can be expected in fusion devices, in comparison to the amorphous solid lithium surface at room temperature. This difference is particularly present at the lowest impact energies (0.025 eV, 300 K) and at a grazing incidence angle. The crystalline and amorphous surfaces do not show significant differences in the sticking and reflection of D atoms if the other conditions of impact angle and Li surface temperature are the same. Energy distributions of the reflected D atoms are linearly dependent on the impact energy, with the gradient (0.25–0.5) mainly dependent on the D incident angle. The average reflected angle of D atoms is spread between 40° and 65° for all considered parameters of the surface and irradiating particles. The D atoms retained in lithium in these simulations are distributed within a few surface monolayers, with the depth strongly depending on the impact angle and energy. The formation of a D adatom layer is predicted for D irradiation at grazing incidence θ = 85°, but the details of this would strongly depend on the accumulation of D in Li. The deuterization of the Li surface could have significant consequences on its physicochemical properties, as has been shown in the past for other materials.36–40 This would certainly influence the retention and reflection of D as well as erosion of the Li surface and will be a subject of our future research.

## Abstract

Lithium wall conditioning has improved the performance of many magnetic fusion devices. Li

conditioning in the RFX-mod device was performed by: (1) a single Li pellet injector and (2)

a multi-Li pellet injector during He plasma discharges; (3) a Li evaporator after He glow

discharge cleaning and He plasma discharge exposure. This report compares the spatial and

depth distributions of Li deposited on polycrystalline graphite witness samples at different

locations in RFX-mod and the elemental and chemical compositions of the resulting surfaces.

The sample surfaces were analyzed ex situ using secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) and

high-resolution X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (HR-XPS). The results showed that Li pellet

injection provided a relatively uniform toroidal coverage while Li evaporation produced highly

localized Li deposition. A Li 1s HR-XPS peak at 56.5 eV binding energy (BE) characteristic

of lithium-intercalated graphite was only observed with the sample exposed to Li evaporation.

All of the samples exhibited a HR-XPS C 1s peak at 285.1-285.2 eV BE that is largely

attributed to hydrogenated graphite. This finding suggests that hydrogenation of fresh graphite

occurs during He plasma discharge exposures. Our results have implications for density control

and the selection of Li conditioning techniques in magnetic fusion devices.

## 1. Introduction

Wall materials inside a magnetic fusion device interact with the plasma and strongly influence

plasma performance. Coating the plasma facing components (PFCs) with Li in a process

referred to as Li conditioning, or lithiumization, has improved plasma performance in devices

such as TFTR [1], T-11M [2], FTU [3], CDX-U [4], NSTX [5], LTX [6], EAST [7], and DIII-

D [8]. Benefits observed after lithiumization include increased confinement time, reduced H

isotope recycling, reduced impurity emissions, and suppressed edge-localized modes (ELMs).

The reduction in H isotope recycling is attributed in part to the high chemical reactivity of Li,

which results in incident H binding to Li, or Li-bound O, rather than recycling back into the

plasma [9–11].

Li conditioning has been performed by a variety of methods across magnetic fusion devices,

with each technique providing varying spatial uniformity and Li injection rates. Methods of

lithiumization include pellet injection [1], powder injection [7,8,12], evaporation [4,6,7,13,14],

liquid lithium limiter (LLL) comprised of a capillary porous system (CPS) [2–4], and flowing

liquid lithium systems [15]. The RFX-mod device has experimented with several Li

conditioning techniques, including a single Li pellet injector (LPI) [16], Li evaporation via a

capillary porous system [17], and a multi-pellet Li injector (MPI) [18].

RFX-mod is a reversed field pinch (RFP) magnetic fusion device of circular cross section and

major/minor radius of 2/0.46 m that operates at high plasma currents up to 2 MA [19]. RFX-

mod does not have a limiter or divertor, resulting in plasmas that interact with the entirety of

the vessel walls. Tiles made of polycrystalline graphite (manufactured by Carbone Lorraine,

type 5890PT) completely cover the first wall of RFX-mod in order to withstand heat loads that

can locally reach tens of MW/m2 [20].

Graphite PFCs are known to retain large quantities of hydrogen [21,22]. Incident H ions and

atoms that are not reflected face a complex transport and chemical environment within the

graphite tiles. Upon implantation, H atoms diffuse along graphitic planes, grain boundaries,

and porous channels and eventually recombine into H2 molecules in the bulk or at the surface

or chemisorb (form chemical bonds) to C atoms in graphitic planes or at defects [21,23–25]. H

chemisorption to graphitic C atoms results in the rehybridization of the sp2-hybridized C-C

bonds to sp3-hybridized C-H bonds [26–31]. The C-H bonds in graphite are stable at room

temperature but can be broken by elevated temperatures (T > 400 K) or by ion bombardment

to yield the desorption of H2 molecules [21,24,25,29,30,32,33].

As graphite PFCs in fusion devices continually accumulate hydrogen and eventually saturate

during plasma discharges, the recycling of H back into the plasma poses problems for density

control. Many fusion devices with graphite PFCs, including RFX-mod, addressed density

control problems by implementing He glow discharge cleaning (GDC) to reduce the H

inventory in the graphite [34–38]. The Li conditioning techniques previously described also

help control plasma density and supplement He GDC. Injected Li is well-known to intercalate

into graphite and is ionized in the process by donating an electron to the delocalized network

of  bonds in graphite [39–42].

Ex situ surface analysis studies used secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) and X-ray

photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to characterize the spatial and depth distribution and

chemical composition of films produced by lithiumization in RFX-mod [18,43]. Similar

investigations of boronization in RFX-mod utilized SIMS, XPS, and Fourier Transform

infrared attenuated total reflection (FTIR-ATR) spectroscopy to demonstrate toroidal

variations in boron film thickness and film stoichiometry related to sample distance from the

boronization glow discharge electrodes [44]. Such RFX-mod sample exposure experiments can

be compared to ex situ surface analysis studies performed utilizing DIII-D’s Divertor Material

Analysis System (DiMES) [45] or the in-vacuo surface analysis studies performed with the

Materials Analysis and Particle Probe (MAPP) on LTX [46] and NSTX [47] or with the Sample

Exposure Probe (SEP) on LTX- [48]. Other studies have used ex situ surface analysis to

investigate the composition or erosion of samples taken directly from multiple PFC tiles after

surface conditioning and plasma exposure in NSTX [49,50] and DIII-D [51].

Our studies presented herein compare the spatial and depth distribution and the final chemical

state of Li films deposited by the LPI, CPS, and MPI lithiumization methods in RFX-mod by

using SIMS and high-resolution XPS (HR-XPS). We describe first an examination of the

spatial and depth distribution of lithium deposition around the RFX-mod torus obtained by

different Li injection techniques. Second, we report on the lithium abundance and elemental

composition of the first wall surfaces. Lastly, chemical interactions of lithium with RFX-mod

graphite and in-vessel and atmospheric impurities were investigated. These results are relevant

to discussions of Li conditioning, density control, and H recycling in magnetic fusion devices

with graphite PFCs, including the newly upgraded RFX-mod: RFX-mod2 [52].

## 2. Materials and methods

2.1. Lithium wall conditioning

In RFX-mod, where particle control is particularly challenging [17], lithiumization was first

introduced with the LPI technique, where right-circular cylindrical (Ø = 1.5 mm, L = 5 mm)

lithium pellets were injected into He plasma discharges for ablation and distribution. Single

lithium pellet injection proved successful by improving density control and overall plasma

performance. The resulting Li coatings were uniform across the vessel. However, many time-

consuming He conditioning discharges were required in order to inject a sufficient amount of

Li [16].

Li evaporation was then tested via a CPS on loan from ENEA-Frascati laboratories, where it

was used in the FTU tokamak as a LLL. A full description of the LLL was given by Alfier et

al. [53]. While in past work the evaporator in RFX-mod was referred to as the LLL, we refer

to it herein as the CPS, since this more clearly reflects the function of the device in this work

as a Li evaporator. Briefly, the CPS is semi-cylindrical in shape with 120 cm2 of surface area.

Li is evaporated by heating the CPS to 450 C. In a given cycle, 1 g of Li can be evaporated in

90-120 mins. Prior to Li evaporation, the PFCs are exposed to extensive He GDC and He

plasma discharges [17]. While the CPS technique deposited orders of magnitude larger mass

of Li than the LPI technique, Li emission lines and initial SIMS measurements demonstrated

that the evaporated Li was highly non-uniform toroidally [17,18].

The latest Li conditioning technique tested, the MPI, sought to achieve the uniform Li coatings

achieved with the LPI technique but at a higher Li injection rate. The MPI was developed by

the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory and was described in detail by Mansfield et al. [54].

The MPI injects 1-mm Li spheres at a frequency of 250 Hz, which translates to 25

mg/discharge. This rate can be compared to the LPI Li injection rate of 4 mg/discharge. Li

emission lines and initial SIMS measurements demonstrated an improved spatial uniformity of

the MPI technique over the CPS technique [18].

Three manipulators enable the exposure of samples to lithium deposition and are located at

three different toroidal positions. These toroidal manipulator positions are referred to as 9D,

11D, and 2D and are depicted in Figure 1. With respect to position 9D, positions 11D and 2D

2.3. Instrumental details

SIMS measurements and depth profiles of the species present were obtained by sputtering the

sample surface using a monoenergetic O2+ primary ion beam (6 keV, collimated to 50-µm dia.)

from a VG Fisons mass-filtered duoplasmatron ion gun (DP50B). The ion beam was rastered

over a 250 x 250-m area. A Hiden SIMS analyzer (EQS1000), using an electrostatic energy

analyzer and a quadrupole mass filter, was used in pulse counting mode for negative and

positive ion detection and collected ions from the central region (approx. 75%) of the rastered

area. At least five depth profiles were conducted on each sample from different locations to

confirm spatial uniformity, and only one of those depth profiles was then reported. The erosion


<!-- Page 6 -->


6

rate, measured by a KLA-Tencor mechanical surface profiler (P-10) with a 2-nm vertical

resolution, was 7 nm/min for the LPI and MPI samples and 27 nm/min for the CPS samples.

HR-XPS measurements, conducted in the Laboratory for Surface Chemistry (LSC) at Princeton

University, were performed in an ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) instrument equipped with a VG

Scienta XPS/UPS/ARPES/ISS hemispherical analyzer (R3000) with a 300-mm radius and a

position-sensitive detector based on a resistive anode channel plate system. A Scienta X-ray

source (MX 650) operated at 450 W and 15 kV and a 7-crystal monochromator provided Al K-

α X-rays (1486.7 eV). Ultimate performance of this instrument gave a Ag 3d5/2 peak with a

full-width-at-half-maximum (FWHM) of 0.60 eV. Samples were mounted on a Mo flag and

transferred to the analysis chamber (2×10-10 Torr). Spectra were obtained using a takeoff angle

of 90° for photoelectrons with respect to the surface plane of the sample. Survey scans of the

samples were obtained at a pass energy, Epass, of 200 eV (300 meV analyzer resolution), while

scans of smaller energy regions were obtained at Epass = 100 eV (150 meV analyzer resolution)

unless otherwise stated. For quantification, sensitivity factors of 0.025, 0.296, and 0.711 for Li

1s, C 1s, and O 1s, respectively, were used [56]. Reported binding energies (BEs) herein are

referenced to Au 4f7/2 at 84.0 eV BE. Sample charging was observed in the lithiated samples

and was corrected by shifting the raw data to align the Si 2p peak, which arises from the

overlapping 2p3/2 and 2p1/2 core lines, in the lithiated samples with the Si 2p peak (103.2 eV

BE) in a reference graphite sample that exhibited no charging. Sample charging in the lithiated

samples ranged from 0.3-0.9 eV. Si was an impurity found in all samples and is most likely

present as SiO2. Our Si 2p peak BE for SiO2 matches previously reported values [57]. Peak

fitting of HR-XPS spectra was performed in CasaXPS. The graphitic carbon C 1s peak was fit

using a Doniach-Šunjić function [58] with the FWHM allowed to vary as a fitting variable. All

other peaks were fit using mixed Gaussian-Lorentzian profiles with the FWHM of all peaks

within a given spectrum set to be equal. A Shirley background was used in all cases [59].

conditioned samples to ensure that the Li isotope signals matched throughout the depth profile.

The 6Li+ and 7Li+ signals match in the LPI 9D sample in Figure 2b but cannot be compared for

the MPI 9D and CPS 9D samples in Figures 2c and 2d, respectively, since at the higher Li

levels in the MPI 9D and CPS 9D samples, the 7Li+ signal saturates the SIMS detector. Hence,

the 6Li+ signal is used to follow the Li depth profiles, as presented later in Figure 3.

The intensities of the 16O+ and 12C+ signals vary between samples and both show a trend of

MPI 9D > LPI 9D > reference graphite > CPS 9D, which matches that found in ref. [18]. The

12C+ intensity in the CPS 9D sample was 1-2 orders of magnitude lower than in the MPI 9D

and LPI 9D samples throughout the top 150 nm. The intensity of the 11B+ signal varied between

the samples with the following trend: MPI 9D > LPI 9D > CPS 9D ≈ reference graphite. The

11B+ signal increased significantly in the LPI and MPI samples as a result of contamination

from previous boron wall conditioning performed in RFX-mod. During the He discharge that

ablates and distributes the Li pellets, B in the graphite PFCs is sputtered and redeposited on the

LPI and MPI samples. The 11B+ signal in the CPS 9D sample remained at a background level

similar to the reference graphite sample since there was no plasma during Li evaporation.

Observation in Figure 2 of varying O, C, and B signals between the different Li conditioning

methods indicates that these samples probed by SIMS had significantly different chemical

environments, although we note that surface roughness and porosity could influence the

measured signals as well. Such different chemical environments, or matrix effects, are known

to cause changes in elemental ion yields, which makes quantifying SIMS data and comparing

elemental signals challenging between chemically different samples [60–62]. Oxygen, which

has a high electron affinity, introduces strong matrix effects in the surface that increase the ion

yield of positive ions. This known matrix effect of oxygen prompts us to evaluate the Li

concentration during the SIMS depth profiles by following the ratio of the 6Li+ signal to the

16O+ signal (6Li+/16O+). This approach has been used in past SIMS studies on RFX-mod samples

in efforts to limit the influence of oxygen matrix effects on depth profiles of Li, C, and B

[18,55]. Given that other unknown matrix effects influence the SIMS data as well, our

discussion of the SIMS results will be largely qualitative.

SIMS analysis of standards of known relevant mixtures of elemental concentrations and depth

profiles to provide calibrations, which was not possible for this report.

The poorer spatial uniformity of Li deposition observed for the MPI technique compared to the

LPI technique matches prior reports [18]. The decrease in spatial uniformity for the MPI

technique was attributed to the lower plasma penetration depth of the smaller Li pellets utilized

with the MPI technique (spherical; Ø = 1 mm) compared to the LPI technique (right-circular

cylindrical; Ø = 1.5 mm, L = 5 mm). High spatial nonuniformity between the CPS samples was

expected from past SIMS and Li influx studies in RFX-mod [17,18]. Innocente et al. reported

that proximity to the Li evaporator resulted in a thick Li film deposited on their 9D graphite

sample and a mixed Li/C film deposited on their 11D graphite sample [18].

By considering the plots shown in Figures 2 and 3, we can qualitatively describe how the

graphite samples were modified by the three Li conditioning techniques. With both the LPI and

MPI techniques, Li pellets are ablated during He discharges, and the resulting Li ions are

transported through the plasma and eventually implant in graphite. The Li concentration in the

graphite peaks within the top 60 nm, with Li intercalating more deeply into the bulk of the

graphite. With the CPS technique, graphite in close proximity to the evaporator (i.e. at position

9D) is coated by a thick layer of Li. Li intercalates into the graphite, but a significant Li film

remains at the graphite surface. In contrast, the CPS 11D sample, 60 away toroidally from the

evaporator, is coated with very little Li. The thin Li coating intercalates into the graphite bulk,

and no appreciable Li film is left at the graphite surface. This conclusion is supported by the

lack of a peak in the CPS 6Li+/16O+ ratio depth profiles and the low 6Li+/16O+ ratio for the CPS

11D sample.

Our assumption that there is a Li film on top of the graphite for the CPS 9D sample is supported

by the 6Li+/16O+ depth profiles in Figure 3a, the lower 12C+ signal for the CPS 9D sample

compared to the LPI 9D and MPI 9D samples in Figure 2, and the lack of a significant 11B+

signal in the CPS 9D sample compared to the LPI 9D and MPI 9D samples in Figure 2. This

proposal also explains several aspects of the B signal in the CPS 9D sample. Since the CPS 9D

sample was exposed to He GDC and He plasmas prior to Li evaporation, B from erosion and

redeposition is likely to be present in the graphite similar to what was seen for the LPI 9D and

MPI 9D samples in Figure 2b and 2c. However, no B signal was observed from the CPS 9D

sample substrate because of attenuation by the Li coating. In contrast, the CPS 11D sample full

Thus, SIMS data indicates qualitatively that pellet injection provided the best toroidal

uniformity, with the LPI technique performing better than the MPI technique. In contrast, Li

3.2. HR-XPS measurements of surface elemental and chemical compositions

HR-XPS (hereafter indicated as XPS for brevity) survey spectra of unexposed graphite from

RFX-mod (used as a reference) and as-received post-exposure lithiated graphite samples are

shown in Figure 4. Each lithiated graphite sample was exposed to Li conditioning at the 9D

sample insertion position that is in the same toroidal section as the LPI and CPS and 30° away

toroidally from the MPI. The XPS survey scans are plotted on an absolute scale and have two

prominent peaks near 532 and 285 eV BE, corresponding to photoelectron emission from the

O 1s and C 1s core levels, respectively. In the lithiated graphite samples, Li (Li 1s, 56 eV BE)

was detected only for the CPS and MPI samples. The Li 1s peak for the MPI sample is difficult

to see at the scale used in Figure 4 but is readily observed in a regional scan in Figure 5. Si (Si

2s, 154 eV BE; Si 2p, 103 eV BE) and Na (Na KLL Auger, 498 eV BE) impurities were

detected for all samples. Na is a known impurity in RFX-mod graphite [44]. The XPS spectrum

from the unused graphite sample was dominated by a single, narrow graphitic C 1s peak at

284.65 eV BE (FWHM 0.7 eV), as shown in a regional XPS scan in Figure 5. XPS spectra

from the lithiated samples have a wider graphitic C peak and additional C peaks indicating

other chemical environments due to oxidized carbon species, which will be discussed further

below. Impurity oxygen in the unused graphite reference sample gave rise to an O 1s peak

centered at 532.9 eV BE. The lithiated samples showed a larger oxygen peak than the graphite

reference, which indicates an increased oxygen concentration at or near the surface due to

oxidation, as described quantitatively below in Table 2.

The surface elemental composition of the unexposed graphite and lithiated graphite samples

was obtained by quantitative XPS analysis and is shown in Table 2. This analysis determined

the average composition of the top several nm of the surface of the analyzed samples assuming

a homogeneous depth distribution of the detected elements. Calculations were carried out using

the expression Ci = (Ii/Si) / i(Ii/Si), where Ci is the concentration (atomic fraction), Ii is the


<!-- Page 11 -->


11

XPS signal intensity for each element, and Si is the atomic sensitivity factor for the measured

elemental core level [56]. The values for Ii were determined by integration of the individual

peak areas after appropriate background subtraction.

Lithium surface abundance was greatest for the CPS sample at 15 at.% Li, while only 3 at.%

Li was measured for the MPI sample. The difference in the amount of surface lithium between

the CPS and MPI samples is consistent with the difference in total injected Li for the two

samples. Li was not detected in the LPI sample by XPS, which was unexpected due to the

larger amount of Li injected with the LPI technique compared to the MPI technique for the

XPS samples (see Table 1). This disparity could again be a result of differences in the ablation,

plasma penetration, and transport of Li pellets in RFX-mod due to differences between the two

Li injection techniques in Li pellet size and the frequency of pellet injection. We note that

SIMS, contrary to XPS, did detect Li in the LPI 9D sample, and B in all of the 9D samples, but

that is not unexpected due to the differences in detection limits for XPS (0.1-1 at.%) and SIMS

(ppm-ppb) and sampling depths for the two techniques.

Oxygen levels in the lithiated graphite samples were notably higher than for the reference

graphite sample. We interpret the higher oxygen concentration in the lithiated samples as the

result of two effects. First, Li acted as a getter for oxygen-containing gases within the RFX-

mod vessel (i.e. H2O) and during sample exposure to ambient air. Second, background oxygen-

containing gases during the He GDC and He plasma discharges oxidized the graphite surface.

As stated above, He GDC and He plasma discharges were performed prior to Li evaporation

with the CPS, and He discharges were the method by which Li pellets were ablated and

transported for the LPI and MPI. While He is inert and thus does not oxidize the surface

directly, oxygen-containing gases increase in the background and are excited and ionized in

the He GDC and He plasma discharges, and so increased interaction and reaction of oxygen

with the initial graphite wall material results in increased oxygen levels in the lithiated graphite

samples.

In order to obtain further information on the chemical nature of the lithiated graphite sample

surfaces, we obtained narrow, regional scans of the XPS O 1s, C 1s, and Li 1s photoelectron

peaks from the lithiated graphite samples. These XPS regional scans for the LPI, MPI, and CPS

samples and the unexposed graphite reference are all presented in Figure 5, along with a

determination of the constituent peaks from decomposition of the overall intensity and

lineshape for each core level spectrum. Table 3 provides the BEs, FWHMs, and assignments

for these constituent peaks. The spectra in Figure 5 are displayed after being normalized to

have the same min to max intensities. All of the spectra were taken at Epass = 100 eV, except

for the LPI Li 1s spectrum, which was taken at Epass = 200 eV. To correct for the increased

intensity due to the two-fold higher pass energy, the intensity of the LPI Li 1s spectrum was

divided by a factor of ten, as intensity is proportional to Epass3.3 in our spectrometer.

In assigning the Li compounds that comprise the deposited Li film surfaces, we consider the

Li 1s spectra together with the C 1s and O1s spectra. A Li 1s peak was detected only for the

CPS and MPI samples. The CPS sample Li 1s peak is asymmetric and was best fit with two

peaks at 55.6 and 56.5 eV BE. Given that all the samples were exposed to ambient air between

Li injection and XPS analysis, surface Li is likely present as Li2CO3 [49,50,63–65]. Thus, for

the CPS sample, we assign the larger Li peak at 55.6 eV BE as due to Li2CO3, which is in close

agreement with reported Li binding energies for Li2CO3 of 55.4-55.5 eV  [64,66]. When

considering the BE separation of the accompanying C 1s and O 1s peaks from the Li 1s peak

for Li2CO3, as described by Wood and Teeter [65], our assignment of Li2CO3 is supported by

C 1s and O 1s peaks at 290.3 and 532.2 eV BE, respectively. Also, the Li 1s, C 1s, and O 1s

peak areas have the proper stoichiometric ratio for Li2CO3 after correction for the sensitivity

factors. We assign the second Li 1s peak in the CPS sample at 56.5 eV to lithium-intercalated

graphite, commonly denoted as LiC6. Assignment of this peak to metallic Li or other oxidized

Li compounds such as Li2O, LiOH, and Li2O2 was not preferred because the Li 1s BEs reported

for these compounds are lower than that of Li2CO3, not higher [40,63–66]. O 1s peaks for Li2O,

LiOH, and Li2O2 that have been reported to be 528.5-531.5 eV BE [42,49,50,64–66], were also


<!-- Page 13 -->


13

absent for the CPS sample. The assignment of the Li 1s BE for LiC6 in Figure 5 is within the

range of previously reported values, which span 55.6-57.2 eV BE [40–42,63]. The

corresponding C 1s peak at 285.1-285.2 eV BE assigned in part to LiC6 for the CPS sample is

also in agreement with prior reports for LiC6 of 285.0-285.2 eV BE [40–42,63]. The MPI

sample Li 1s spectrum can be fit with a single peak at 55.6 eV BE and is also assigned to

Li2CO3, with consistent C 1s and O 1s peaks at 290.3 and 532.2 eV BE, respectively.

Next, we discuss in more detail the C 1s spectra. Carbon shows the widest range of XPS peaks

of the three elements presented here due to the wide variety of oxidation states possible (+4 to

-4) and the roughly one-volt shift of the C 1s peak associated with each change. The CPS

sample has a large C 1s peak at 290.3 eV BE assigned to Li2CO3. While every sample has a

prominent peak at 285.1-285.2 eV BE, carbon in LiC6 definitively contributes to this peak only

in the CPS sample, as determined by the LiC6 component in its Li 1s spectrum. On the low BE

side of the C 1s lineshape, each sample has a narrow peak at 284.3-284.4 eV BE that we assign

to graphitic carbon [40–42,49,63,67]. The graphitic carbon peak BE in the lithiated samples is

slightly lower than that for the unused graphite reference, which is located at 284.65 eV BE.

This observation could be explained by either a difference in cleaving of the graphite samples

[67] or structural changes induced during He GDC/He plasma discharges [68]. We also

observed a link between the intensity and the FWHM of the graphitic carbon peak. In the

reference graphite and MPI samples, the graphitic carbon peak was prominent and narrow with

0.7 eV FWHM. In the CPS and LPI samples, the graphitic carbon peak had a FWHM of 0.9

and 1.1 eV, respectively, and appeared as a shoulder to the larger peak at 285.1-285.2 eV BE.

Prior studies have reported broadening of the C 1s peak of highly ordered pyrolytic graphite

(HOPG) and polycrystalline graphite due to Ar+ ion bombardment [44,67,69]. We therefore

propose that the difference in the intensity and FWHMs of the graphitic carbon peaks between

the three lithiated graphite samples is in part a result of varying plasma conditions or exposure

times/fluxes during He GDC/He plasma discharges.

The He GDC/He plasma discharges also had the effect of hydrogenating the surface carbon by

reaction with excited, ionized, and/or dissociated H2 and H2O background gas molecules in the

RFX-mod vessel. The growth of an XPS peak from hydrogenated carbon in graphite and carbon

nanotubes after hydrogenation (i.e. by hydrogen plasma, H atom source, or Birch reduction) is

well-documented with the peak at 285.1-285.5 eV BE (+0.6-1.0 eV BE relative to graphitic

carbon/C-C sp2-hybridized bonds) [26–29,70,71]. We therefore assign the C 1s peak at 285.1-


<!-- Page 14 -->

285.2 eV BE in all lithiated graphite samples to be in part due to hydrogenated graphite, in the

range of prior reports. We also add that a final contribution to the C 1s peak at 285.1-285.2 eV

BE could be from adventitious carbon contamination that occurs from air exposure prior to

analysis. Adventitious carbon is typically reported to be at 284.8-285.0 eV BE. While this BE

is slightly lower in BE than the peak at 285.1-285.2 eV, the adventitious carbon could be a

small contribution that is within the peak envelope but unresolvable.

We note that the reference graphite sample was not exposed to any He GDC or He plasma

discharges and does not exhibit a significant signal at 285.1-285.2 eV BE. As such, we did not

include the hydrogenated graphite peak in the fitting for the reference graphite. However, the

reference graphite fitting required an additional peak at 285.0 eV BE. This peak at 285.0 eV

BE is consistent with prior XPS studies of pristine or reference graphite where a peak near this

location was assigned to a “defect peak” [72] or “disordered carbon” [67]. The reference

graphite also has a small peak at 290.9 eV BE assigned to the well-documented →*

transition satellite [67,72]. The remaining C 1s peaks (in all samples) at 285.7-285.8, 286.5-

286.6, 287.4, and 288.8-288.9 eV BE were assigned to carbon in carbon-oxygen functional

groups as per the XPS C 1s model presented in López et al. (see Table 3) [73]. For carbon-

oxygen functional groups with multiple C atoms, the C atom for the assignment in Table 3 is

indicated by an underline. We fitted the total sensitivity factor-corrected areas of the carbon-

oxygen functional group C 1s and O 1s peaks such that the C/O ratios were within reasonable

agreement (C/O between 0.75-1).

Finally, we discuss the O 1s spectra in additional detail. The overall O 1s lineshapes were

decomposed into a combination of four or five peaks as shown in Figure 5 and described in

*Table 3. The CPS and MPI sample O 1s peaks include a Li2CO3 contribution at 532.2 eV BE*

with a stoichiometrically determined area based on the sensitivity factor-corrected areas of their

corresponding Li 1s and C 1s peaks. The remaining four peaks used in the fittings at 531.1-

531.2, 532.0-532.1, 532.9-533.0, and 533.9 eV BE were assigned to oxygen in carbon-oxygen

functional groups. While the O 1s XPS peak for oxidized carbon is often fit with only two or

three broad peaks due to lack of sufficient peak structure to guide the fitting [67,74,75], small

shoulders on the low and high BE sides of the O 1s spectra warranted the utilization of four

oxidized carbon components. As such, we followed the more granular O 1s fitting utilized in

Kwan et al. (see Table 3) [76]. For carbon-oxygen functional groups with multiple O atoms,

the O atom for the assignment in Table 3 is indicated by an underline.

An unforeseen outcome of our HR-XPS regional scans of the lithiated samples was the clear

identification of the hydrogenated carbon peak at 285.1-285.2 eV BE from the graphitic carbon

peak at 284.3-284.4 eV BE in the C 1s spectra. While there are likely other contributions to the

intensity at or near the hydrogenated carbon peak (i.e. LiC6 in the CPS sample), our data

suggests a significant amount of the graphite in the top several nm is hydrogenated by the He

GDC and He discharges before any exposure to H-fueled discharges. The source of H could be

either H-containing residual vacuum gasses, i.e. H2 or H2O, or H that is sputtered and

redeposited from the surrounding H-containing, graphite PFCs of RFX-mod [77,78].

This observation of hydrogenation may seem counterintuitive as He GDC and He discharges

are known to reduce the net H content of graphite PFCs in RFX-mod and other fusion devices.

However, we again make the important distinction that our samples, contrary to fusion device

PFCs, had not yet been exposed to any H plasmas prior to He plasma exposure. Therefore, in

RFX-mod, He GDC/He discharges have the net effect of hydrogenating fresh graphite while

reducing, but not eliminating, H levels in H plasma-exposed graphite PFCs. Prior investigations

reported that increasing intensities of He ion bombardment [79] or baking [80] were required

to remove increasing amounts of H in graphite. Our XPS results suggest that He GDC/He

discharges in RFX-mod do not efficiently remove all of the tightly bound H in the graphite


<!-- Page 16 -->


16

tiles, which leaves sufficient hydrogenated graphite to generate the XPS peak at 285.1-285.2

eV BE. If the graphite surfaces in RFX-mod are assumed to be partially hydrogenated at all

times, it is important to consider that Li intercalates at twice the rate in H-containing graphite

than H-free graphite [39].

Separately, the coexistence of Li2CO3 and LiC6 in the CPS XPS sample has important

implications. We know already from previous reports that Li2CO3 readily forms on the surface

of Li and Li compounds (i.e. Li2O, LiOH) when exposed to air. Our samples were exposed to

air briefly during transfer from RFX-mod to the vacuum transfer module and again during

transfer from the vacuum transfer module to our HR-XPS chamber. The continued presence of

LiC6 in the sampling depth of our XPS measurements suggests that either (1) the Li2CO3 forms

an outer surface layer that grows to a finite depth and eventually acts as a diffusion barrier to

the reactant species H2O, CO2, and Li or (2) LiC6 is exposed through cracks in the Li2CO3 film

or cluster formation of Li2CO3. The coexistence of Li2CO3 and LiC6 XPS peaks after LiC6 was

exposed to a controlled, one-minute air exposure was previously reported [63]. In that study, a

detailed analysis of surface structure or morphology was not performed, but Ar+ ion sputtering

of the air-exposed LiC6 resulted in the removal of the Li2CO3 XPS peak. The CPS XPS sample

in our study shows that LiC6 remains in the top several nm of Li-exposed graphite even after

approximately one hour of air exposure.

## 4. Conclusions

This study used ex situ SIMS and XPS analysis to characterize and compare three

lithiumization techniques in RFX-mod by investigating the final elemental and chemical

compositions, depth profiles, and spatial uniformity of the surfaces resulting from Li

depositions on graphite samples. SIMS analysis determined that Li depositions were the most

uniform from the LPI technique, slightly less uniform from the MPI technique, and highly non-

uniform from the CPS technique. The LPI and MPI techniques appeared to implant Li into

graphite, while the CPS technique evaporated a Li film on top of the graphite with the thickness

highly dependent on proximity to the evaporator. With all of the techniques, Li intercalated

deep into the bulk of the graphite samples. Both SIMS and XPS analyses demonstrated that the

highest Li quantities were found in samples exposed to the CPS technique in the region closest

to the evaporator, followed by samples exposed to the MPI technique, and then the LPI

technique. Our SIMS results for the LPI and MPI techniques suggest that the spatial uniformity

of Li deposition in the torus improves with increasing Li pellet size, agreeing with prior reports.


<!-- Page 17 -->


17

We detected Li with XPS only in samples exposed to the MPI and CPS techniques. The XPS

spectra for the MPI and CPS samples exhibited peaks characteristic of Li2CO3, which formed

at the surface after sample exposure to atmospheric air. Our understanding of the chemical state

of surface Li in the RFX-mod vessel is convoluted by the observed formation of Li2CO3 in

atmospheric air, which supports the utilization of in vacuo surface analysis for Li plasma

material interactions studies. Peaks assigned to LiC6 in the Li 1s and C 1s XPS spectra were

only evident in the CPS sample. All of the lithiated samples showed evidence of hydrogenated

graphite, yet none of these samples were exposed to H-fueled plasma discharges. However,

each sample was exposed to He-fueled GDC or plasma discharges either during Li injection

(LPI and MPI techniques) or before Li evaporation (CPS technique). Given this sample history,

our results suggest that He GDC/He plasma discharges can hydrogenate fresh graphite samples,

which were previously unexposed to any plasma or Li conditioning. We propose that this

hydrogenation occurs via the bombardment of the fresh graphite sample surface with excited,

ionized, and/or dissociated H-containing gases (i.e. H2, H2O) from the residual vacuum or that

are evolved from the graphite tiles during He+ ion bombardment. The observed hydrogenation

in all of the XPS samples indicates that there are high levels of H in the RFX-mod vessel prior

to Li conditioning. In order to improve density control and the cleanliness of the injected or

evaporated Li, thereby improving plasma performance, we suggest more extensive He GDC or

He plasma discharge exposure before Li conditioning is performed.

Preventing Increased Air Pollution in Pennsylvania’s Environmental Justice Communities Ryan A Chaban1, Daniel W. Dudt2, Bethany Gordon3, Evan T. Ostrowski4

1William & Mary, Department of Physics, Williamsburg, VA

2Princeton University, Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Princeton, NJ 3University of Virginia, Department of Engineering Systems and Environment, Charlottesville, VA 4Princeton University, Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Princeton, NJ https://doi.org/10.38126/JSPG180407 Corresponding author: bmg6bt@virginia.edu Keywords: environmental justice; air pollution; health disparities; climate policy; cap-and-trade; RGGI; Pennsylvania

Executive Summary: Air pollutants are known to cause serious health impacts, and historically marginalized groups are disproportionately exposed to these risks. Other hazardous pollutants often accompany carbon dioxide emissions during fossil fuel combustion, and therefore reductions in greenhouse gas emissions from climate policy can also improve air quality. However, although these policies may reduce pollution overall, existing programs have often increased local emissions levels – particularly in the most overburdened neighborhoods. The adverse health effects caused by a redistribution of emissions must be considered as Pennsylvania plans to join the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative. We recommend the Department of Environmental Protection include an annual impact assessment of their cap-and-trade program on vulnerable communities using both the available carbon dioxide emissions data and additional local air quality measurements. I. Statement of issue i. Air pollution is particularly harmful to Environmental Justice communities Pennsylvania’s long history of using coal and natural gas for power generation has not only contributed to carbon dioxide (CO2) pollution but has also expelled significant amounts of other pollutants (Clean Air Council, n.d.). These pollutants include NOx, SOx, VOCs, PM2.5, and air toxics 1 , and are known to contribute to adverse health effects (Clean Air Council, n.d.; Abelsohn and Stieb 2011; Wellbery 2017). Sources of air pollution are often located in resource-constrained and racially segregated areas, causing disproportionate health effects for marginalized groups (“Tracking and Evaluation of

1NOx (Nitrous Oxides), SOx  (Sulfur Oxides), VOC (Volatile Organic Compounds),  PM2.5  (Particulate Matter 2.5 μm)

Benefits and Impacts of Greenhouse Gas Limits in Disadvantaged Communities: Initial Report” 2017; California EPA 2017; Cushing et al. 2018; “Cap and Trade: More Pollution for the Poor and People of Color” 2019; FWW 2021; Miranda et al. 2011). These communities that face disproportionate exposure and increased vulnerability to environmental harms, including air pollution, are called overburdened communities or Environmental Justice (EJ) communities (US EPA 2016). Their well-being, in the context of new Pennsylvania (PA) climate regulations, is the focus of this analysis. The negative health impacts of air pollution exposure can manifest more severely in individuals who are vulnerable due to extrinsic factors, such as ethnicity

or socioeconomic status (Ostro et al. 2006; Solomon et al. 2012). For example, these vulnerable groups may have less access to preventative healthcare, to fresh food, and to residences located away from major emitters (Tung et al. 2017). As a result, overburdened communities experience short-term (exacerbation of pre-existing respiratory and cardiovascular conditions) and long-term (development of new respiratory and cardiovascular disease, harm to fetal development, and increased mortality) health impacts of air pollution (Abelsohn and Stieb 2011; Smith et al. 2013; Wellbery 2017; Backes et al. 2013). These underlying conditions are also co-morbidities of the current COVID-19 pandemic, putting additional strain on these communities (Wu et al. 2020). Even within regulatory limits, several of the air pollutants responsible for these negative health effects can have a quantifiable impact (Di et al. 2017). As these pollutants correlate with CO2 emissions, it can be beneficial to address EJ air pollution concerns simultaneously with climate regulations targeting greenhouse gases (Cushing et al. 2018; Ostro et al. 2006; Burney 2020). As Pennsylvania moves to enact a CO2 Budget Trading Program and join the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI), the state should consider strengthening the EJ considerations in the bill. Some states who already participate in RGGI have needed to take post-factum action to address an uneven air pollution reduction that has disadvantaged EJ communities. In the following sections, we discuss the implications of an inequitable cap-and-trade system, the current status of the rulemaking in question, and our recommendations for how to move forward in a just way. ii. Cap-and-trade systems could exacerbate disparities in air pollution exposure Cap-and-trade systems, such as RGGI, are a marketbased tool for reducing anthropogenic sources of greenhouse gases in a particular region by setting a limit on CO2 emissions and requiring emitters within that region to purchase an allowance for every unit of CO2 that they emit. Allowances are either bought at regular auctions or traded between regulated facilities. By design, the total CO2 emissions in a capand-trade region should decline with time, as was observed in the current RGGI states (RGGI 2019) and California (CA) (CARB 2019), which has its own capand-trade system. However, the redistribution of

emissions in a cap-and-trade region can lead to winners and losers at the local level. In fact, several studies on both the RGGI (Chan and Morrow 2019; FWW 2021; McKeown 2020) and CA (Cushing et al. 2018) cap-and-trade systems identified that emissions of CO2 and its co-pollutants increased from many facilities near EJ communities after the introduction of the cap-and-trade system (Figure 1). We note that the literature on the EJ consequences of CA’s cap-and-trade system is mixed, with other reports showing positive outcomes in the state (Hernandez-Cortes and Meng 2020) or being inconclusive (California EPA 2017).

Existing regulations and programs of the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) are unlikely to mitigate disparate impacts resulting from a cap-and-trade system. As mandated by the Clean Air Act, the EPA regulates air quality across the country by setting national ambient air quality standards for criteria pollutants and monitoring pollution levels at state-operated air quality testing stations (CFR 40.50). However, the relatively low spatial distribution of air quality monitoring stations does not effectively detect local “hot spots” (Fowlie et al. 2019) of air pollution and can lead to underregulation or over-regulation of certain regions by the EPA (Hsiang et al.  2019; Fowlie et al. 2020; Carlson 2018). In PA, which has sixty-five total air monitoring stations operating in thirty-eight of sixtyseven counties (Wolf and McDonnell 2020), local pollution hot spots potentially generated after capand-trade implementation might not be detected nor trigger a regulatory response by the EPA. Local testing and community monitoring of air quality can be crucial to filling in this missing data (Solomon et al. 2012; Fowlie et al. 2020; Snyder et al. 2013).

The EPA is actively working towards improving EJ outcomes (EPA 2021) and continues to fund innovative projects to investigate creative solutions to state and tribal pollution issues (US EPA ORD 2020a). For example, the EPA is partnering with the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection to study the effectiveness of a low-cost air sensor network monitored by citizen scientists for detection of air pollution hot spots (US EPA ORD 2020b). Rather than wait for stronger EJ guidelines from the EPA or the federal government, some states are moving ahead with EJ legislation of their own. In order to address EJ concerns in CA, the state passed Assembly Bill 617 in 2017 (Garcia 2017). AB 617 takes a community-focused approach to combating air pollution in vulnerable neighborhoods by identifying regions with high cumulative exposure to air pollutants and empowering their local air district to build out local air quality testing capabilities and develop and execute a community emissions reduction plan (Garcia 2017). While still too early in its implementation for proper evaluation, AB 617 has put a spotlight on EJ in CA and how it relates to local air quality testing and community involvement (Fowlie et al. 2020). PA could also consider taking a similar, state-level approach to protect overburdened communities from increased air pollution as the state joins RGGI. II. Political and legal status On October 3, 2019, Governor Tom Wolf signed an executive order (Wolf 2020) that required the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) to develop a proposed rulemaking package to join RGGI and present it to the Environmental Quality Board (EQB). The Wolf administration claimed to have the authority to join RGGI under the Clean Air Act (Clean Air Act 1970), but many politicians viewed this action as executive overreach. In response, the PA General Assembly then passed House Bill 2025 (PA HB20205 2019) which stated that legislative approval is required to enact a price or fee on carbon, therefore effectively preventing the Wolf administration from joining RGGI unilaterally. The Governor vetoed this bill on September 24, 2020 (Wolf 2020), and the General Assembly did not have the required twothirds majority in each chamber to override the veto. Legal challenges to the regulation are also expected, but legal scholars anticipate the Governor’s authority would be upheld (Morris 2020).

As it stands, the DEP is expected to submit the final regulation to the EQB and Independent Regulatory Review Commission for approval by the end of 2021, and Pennsylvania is on track to join RGGI in 2022. While participating in this regional cap-and-trade system will benefit PA air quality through the reductions of CO2 emissions and increased revenue for the Clean Air Fund, the regulation currently does not include language to mitigate any adverse impacts on vulnerable communities that could arise from the program. It is urgent to take protective measures to address the potential EJ concerns while the final regulations are still malleable. III. Policy options The following policy options focus on 25 PA Code Chapter 145 Section 306, which establishes standard requirements for the CO2 Budget Trading Program. i. Option 1: No changes to proposed rulemaking §145.306 would be implemented as currently drafted in the proposed regulation, without any revisions. Advantages Not having additional reporting requirements reduces the regulatory burden on emitters and the administrative responsibilities of the DEP. This could translate into money saved for both investors and taxpayers. Less regulatory oversight and market intervention could also allow CO2 credits to be traded more freely, so that the carbon market can run efficiently and generate the lowest prices. Disadvantages Neglecting to require any assessment of the impacts of the cap-and-trade program on air quality fails to address the potential EJ issues caused by this regulation. Marginalized communities could experience increased air pollution without a method to identify and rectify the situation built into the regulatory infrastructure. This could result in detrimental and long-term effects on public health. ii. Option 2: Annual air quality impact assessment using CO2 emissions data Amend §145.306 to include an annual assessment determining whether any regions are disproportionately affected by increased air pollution as a result of the cap-and-trade program. The DEP would use the CO2 emissions measurements recorded and reported to them by existing procedures to

assess these impacts and publish their findings to the public. This approach is already being considered by the DEP following a public comment period (McDonnell 2021). Advantages This reporting requirement would help address the EJ concerns of RGGI by monitoring its impact on an annual basis. If alarming trends do arise, the public would be aware of the issue and remedial action could be taken. This option would use the CO2 emissions data that is already being reported in the proposed rulemaking, so the additional regulatory burden on emitters would be minimal. CO2 is wellcorrelated with other harmful pollutants so the report would be based on a descriptive, yet coarse, data set (Cushing et al. 2018; Ostro et al. 2006; Burney 2020). Disadvantages This annual report would increase the administrative responsibilities of the DEP, which would demand more government resources to complete. It also increases the likelihood of market intervention, which could result in the carbon market underperforming economic theory and modeling (PA DEQ 2020). Furthermore, only using CO2 emissions data from the budget sources may not adequately resolve the real effects of air pollution on surrounding communities. iii. Option 3: Annual air quality impact assessment with expanded testing Amend §145.306 to include the annual assessment from Option 2, with the additional requirement that the DEP identify a selection of overburdened communities and facilitate local air quality testing of co-pollutants in those communities to supplement the CO2 emissions data. Advantages In addition to the advantages of the annual air quality

impact assessment discussed in Option 2, the local air quality monitoring in pre-selected, vulnerable areas will allow for improved spatial resolution and accuracy in the determination of air quality near RGGI-regulated facilities. This policy option incorporates aspects of CA’s AB 617 to better inform the DEP on remedial modifications to the cap-andtrade policy, if necessary. Low-cost (Caubel et al. 2019; Lin et al. 2020) or mobile air quality sensors (Apte et al. 2017) and the leveraging of citizen scientists (Commodore et al. 2017) make execution of this plan more realistic than in the past. These local testing efforts can be funded by EPA innovation project grants or RGGI auction proceeds since each state has discretion over its own program revenue (RGGI 2020). Disadvantages Potential government intervention in the carbon market could have unintended consequences, as already mentioned in the disadvantages of Option 2. The additional regulation of identifying vulnerable areas and implementing local air quality monitoring would further increase the administrative responsibilities of the DEP and demands on government resources. Lastly, many view local air pollution and climate change mitigation as two separate problems that could both be better served by their own policy approaches (Fowlie et al. 2020). IV. Policy recommendation We recommend that the Department of Environmental Protection incorporate Option 3 into the final rulemaking of their CO2 Budget Trading Program (25 PA. CODE CH. 145). Pennsylvania’s imminent entry into the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative poses a risk to the health of Environmental Justice communities in the state. Now is the time to incorporate meaningful safeguards for the most vulnerable populations in PA and set an example for other RGGI states.
